1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 1,048 kWh (58,961 − 57,913), line items sum to $182.92 ($18.79 + $24.76 + $139.37), and the change versus last month is −$23.60 ($182.92 − $206.52); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map both billing periods to AEP Ohio tariffs by date: last month (2026-07-23 to 2026-08-23) and current (2026-08-23 to 2026-09-22) both fall entirely under the post-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.788; tier-1 blended $0.1677638/kWh for the first 2,000 kWh), so there is no rate change and price_usd = 0.

3. Compute days_usd from the period length: 30 days versus 31 days (−1 day); value that day at last month’s average daily bill or the tariff’s daily baseline, keeping the sign consistent with the total change.

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 300 / HDD 0) to current (CDD 281.5 / HDD 5), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective variable rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly −$23.60; this captures household usage changes not explained by price, days, or weather.

6. Check for a billing error: model the current period with the tariff (fixed $18.788 + 1,048 kWh × $0.1677638 ≈ $194.60) and compare to the actual $182.92; if the difference exceeds rounding, set billing_error_suspected = true and billing_error_usd to the discrepancy (about $11.68), otherwise false and null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
